### base metals: Weak performance and diminished prospects lead to Widespread trimming of price expectations Whilst economic indicators have underwhelmed on a global basis, and the eurozone remains in the doldrums, it is perhaps the manifest slowdown in china which is most troubling to the commodities community. This weakening had been well flagged by many, including Thomson reuters GFms, but nevertheless has been central to a recent widespread downward revision to the outlook and price forecasts for many commodities, including base metals. The chinese government has evidently seen this coming, having already lowered its target GDP growth for 2012 to 7.5%. additionally, the last two months’ major data releases have been pre-empted by interest rate cuts of 25 and 31 basis points, respectively. There is no doubt that more easing is to come, given, as we have previously commented, that falling inflation allows increased room to manoeuvre. Following 7.6% for second quarter GDP growth, this implies that the chinese economy would have to exceed an average 7.2% in the second half of the year to realise or beat the annual target. having earlier alluded to the need to downwardly adjust our price forecasts, as the first half of 2012 has underperformed versus expectations whilst the second half will be starting from a lower base, we have formally

done so in this month’s Base metals one year Forecast report. We are not alone, as the analytical community has virtually wholesale re-rated the base metals outlook downwards, as evidenced by Thomson reuters’ recent Base metals Price Poll. comparing our newly adjusted numbers to the mean forecasts, we see that the 7% cut in our aluminium price forecast for 2012, to $2,045/tonne, compares to the poll’s average of $2,068/tonne. our 5% downward revision to the copper price for this year, to $8,020/tonne compares to $7,999/tonne; our new lead price of $2,000/tonne (-11%) compares to $2,034/tonne; nickel, at $17,750/tonne (-6%) compares to $18,108/tonne; tin, at $21,000/tonne (-12%) compares to $21,041/tonne and zinc, at $1,945/tonne (-5%) compares to $1,972/tonne. as can be seen, Thomson reuters GFms’s revised forecasts are generally slightly lower than consensus, but are not too divergent, ranging between +0.3% (copper) and -2% (nickel) from the poll means. our, and the market’s outlook for 2013, has also weakened, especially as any significant action on quantitative easing in the us and china has not been forthcoming so far, and the delay is weighing on investor sentiment. Downward revisions to our first half 2013 price forecasts are of similar magnitudes to those made for this year, ranging between -3% (copper) and -14% (tin). also, like the rest of the market in general, we are still anticipating that prices for all base metals will show improvements in the latter part of this year and through 2013, as not only demand improves and market balances tighten, but more Qe is implemented. certainly, market fundamentals continue to play second fiddle to macro concerns. across the board, we expect average prices in the first half of next year to exceed 2012 full year averages by 4-8%. ###### Base meTals & oTher commoDiTy Prices ###### Base meTal Prices iN maJor curreNcies 300

##### economic indicatoRs The overall oecD indicator has remained static since February, but dipped slightly to 100.3 in may. most of the individual country oecD leading economic indicators fell slightly or were unchanged. one notable exception was that for Brazil, which rose from 99.0 to 99.2 in may. This was despite other mostly bearish economic data emanating from the country in recent months. Whilst the eurozone indicator remained steady, there was a slight dip for Germany in may. consumer confidence in the us and european economies continued to slide. The eurozone economic sentiment indicator registered its third consecutive fall to 89.9 in June, from 94.5 in march. us consumer confidence has fallen from its 71.6 peak in February to 62.0 in June. however, this wasn’t consistent with the improvement in us light vehicle sales, following the disappointing may data. in Brazil, where economic prospects have weakened, consumer confidence fell to 121.0 from 124.9 in may. expectations appear to be more positive in Japan, where confidence has generally been on an upward trend since the second quarter of 2011. The ism purchasing managers’ index fell sharply in June to 49.7, from 53.5 in may, and was lower than market expectations. it is also the first time that the index has fallen below 50 (which indicates a contraction in factory activity) since July 2009. Further slippage in this index could heighten the prospects of further quantitative easing in the united states, on the back of recessionary fears. The forward-looking new orders component dropped to 47.8 in June, the lowest since april 2009, from 60.1 in may. it was also the largest monthly drop since october 2001, following the september 11 attacks. exports also sank to 47.5, from 53.5 in may. The employment component was relatively better, falling to 56.6 in June from 56.9 the previous

month. having fallen by 1.1% in april, eurozone industrial production (iP) recovered by 0.6%, month-on-month, in may. This was helped by rebounds in most of the major european economy iP numbers; German iP was 1.6% higher in may, month-on-month, after sinking by 2.1% in april; italian iP rose by 0.8% in may, having slipped 2.0% in april. France, however, remained out of sync, posting a 1.9% fall in iP in may, following a 1.4% increase in april. The eurozone Pmi remained steady at 45.1 in June, still indicating contraction in most of the constituent countries, but arresting, for now, the decline seen over the first half of 2012. chinese indicators continue to expose a slowdown in the country’s economy, especially the second quarter GDP release of 7.6% (from 8.1% in the first quarter), the slowest growth in three years. chinese industrial production eased slightly to 9.5% year-on-year in June, and again undershot the consensus expectation. second quarter iP averaged below 9.5%, compared to almost 11.6% for the first quarter. The chinese Pmi eased again in June, to 48.2, although fixed asset investment edged higher to 20.4% for the first half of the year, from 20.1% through may. Within the overall Fai, there were improvements in investment in power and railways and transport, but real estate investment weakened in June. also, whilst domestic investment was slightly higher, there was a sharp fall in foreign investment. Further highlighting the weakening economic conditions were the ongoing fall in retail sales, to 13.7% in June from 13.8% in may and sliding inflation; cPi was 2.2% in June, compared to 3.0% in may. as we alluded to last month, the government did, however, preempt this raft of softer data with another interest rate cut on 5th July, of 31 basis points. oecD leaDiNG iNDicaTor & Base meTals iNDeX ###### chiNese iP GroWTh & Base meTals iNDeX 105 Thomson Reuters GFMS 400

### ALUMINIUM ###### recent developments ###### outlook for the next twelve months **•** **_Fears of a Chinese slowdown were confirmed by the report that second quarter growth registered 7.6%. However, this was far from a worst case scenario. Allied to a slew of weaker economic data from the country, the reasons for the earlier interest rate cut (for the second time in as many months) were clear; another pre-emptive strike by the Chinese authorities. It is also likely that more measures are on the way._** **•** **_Global

reported stocks continue to edge lower, in spite of a consensus view that the market is in surplus. Only the latest Japanese port data showed an increase (the first since January), but even this was attributed to higher imports in a tight spot market, rather than any fall in demand._** **•** **_The underperformance of aluminium, and many (industrial) commodity markets in general, during the first half of the year, has led the majority of the analytical community to lower their price forecasts for this year and next. We have previously flagged the relative weakness versus earlier expectations, but have formally revised our supply/ demand outlook and price forecasts in this month’s report._** **•** **_We now anticipate an increased surplus for this year, of 416,000 tonnes, compared to our previous forecast of 373,000 tonnes. Also, we expect the market to continue in surplus, albeit a lesser one, into 2013. As such, we have lowered our average cash price forecast for 2012 by 7% to $2,045/tonne._** **•** **_The ongoing tightness in availability of spot material has continued to push physical premiums higher in all regions. European duty-paid quotes are around $30/tonne greater than last month, at $250-270/tonne. Japanese spot premiums are $35-40/tonne higher at $230-235/tonne and US Midwest quotes have increased by 0.5¢/lb to 10.5-11¢/lb._** **•** **_Although falling prices and rising costs have led to expectations that global output would come under pressure, this has not been the case so far. Indeed, China alone has pushed production higher, even as the rest of the world has eased lower. Also, government support (in a climate where there is pressure to maintain economic and industrial growth and preserve jobs) appears to be aiding threatened capacity in China and elsewhere._** ###### thomson reuters Gfms’ forecast scenarIos **Base Case, 45% Probability** represents what thomson reuters Gfms consider the most likely outcome for the markets. **Scenario B, 30% Probability** faster recovery than under our base case in the near term and stronger growth thereafter. **Scenario C, 25% Probability** the crisis in the eurozone spreads to cause a markedly slower recovery in the mature economies and a moderation in chinese growth. ###### alumInIum supply-demand balance and prIce forecast ###### Quarterly alumInIum prIce forecast |(000 tonnes)

###### market background It never rains, but it pours. whilst that has been true of the british summer, it also seems to hold for macro and economic data recently. china’s recently reported second quarter Gdp growth rate of 7.6% was not by any means a worst case number, but it did highlight the slowdown evident in the main powerhouse for global commodities. focus in europe has shifted (back) to spain and Italy and the recent libor scandal has put the banking sector (which is crucial for credit, the oil that lubricates a fullyfunctioning commodity market) back in regulators’ sights, adding to the market’s anxiety. the chinese government cut interest rates for the second time in as many months, this time lowering the benchmark one-year lending rate by 31 basis points. the announcement once again pre-empted less positive economic data. this time, Gdp, cpI, retail sales and Ip growth rates for June all edged lower, while faI was only slightly higher, than the previous month. falling inflation, especially in light of lower Gdp and Ip, does imply that further liquidity injections and monetary easing are likely. certainly, the market expects more cuts in the interest rate and banks’ reserve ratios. ###### expectations of more Qe globally have certainly contributed to underlying support. nevertheless, pressures from a weak demand and macro environment have pushed aluminium prices down to a recent low of $1,811/tonne in late June, on an official cash basis. at the time of writing, the cash price was trading around $1,870/tonne, 5% down over the year. ###### total reported inventories down for year-to-date stocks of aluminium in lme warehouses continued to fall during June (down 94,550 tonnes over the month) and into early July. there were some net additions to inventories subsequently, but further outflows see the total at the weekly chanGe In lme stocks vs spot prIce 60000 2300

###### supply response remains limited 

in our previous report, we noted that the high cost chinese nickel pig iron production had provided a cushion to the established producers in the west.  although there have been some reductions in nickel pig iron (npi) output, this is in direct response to lower demand from the chinese stainless steel mills and does not in itself negate the still looming oversupply in the market. 

over the last month, there has been further evidence concerning the changing cost structure within the npi sector. it also highlights the key point being that closure of high cost blast furnace capacity is being offset by new lower-cost eaf-based output.  also, chinese stainless mills are backwardly integrating into npi.  an example of this is the tsingshan Group that is commissioning rotary kiln electric furnace technology to produce nickel pig iron at significantly lower production costs.  all three plants have capacity to produce 25,000 tpy of nickel in pig iron and all three feed tsingshan’s own mills.  xinan stainless is also building an rkef nickel pig iron production plant in beihai, which will produce 36,000 tpy of nickel pig iron. 

the government of china’s inner mongolia province will provide discounts on electricity prices to the npi sector. the subsidies – which may be worth about 100 yuan per tonne of nickel contained – are aimed at propping up loss-making plants in order to save jobs and support the local economy.  the producers already have low power costs; however, this is offset by high transport costs given the inland location.  the region accounts for around one third of chinese nickel production.  china’s nickel pig iron production remained high at 24,953 tonnes in June, down just 1.9% from previous month.
